passage: In a small flat in Marseille, five-year-old Clara wrestles with her boot buckle. "I do it!" she snaps when her mother, Rania, kneels to help. The buckle won't close. Clara's chin wobbles; she turns her face to the wall and scrubs her eyes with her sleeve. When Rania opens her arms, Clara steps back. Rania stays kneeling. "Buckles are hard. I'll wait here in case you want a hand." Clara tries twice more. Then, without looking up, she pushes one foot toward her mother.

qa.q: What was Clara trying to close?
qa.a: She was trying to close her boot buckle.

qa.q: Why might Clara turn to the wall and scrub her eyes?
qa.a: She seems to be hiding her tears, perhaps so no one sees that she is upset or needs help.

qa.q: Which of Rania's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: She stayed kneeling and offered help without pushing a hug, so Clara could accept it in her own way.

qa.q: What is it like for Rania when Clara steps back from her open arms?
qa.a: It may sting a little, but she stays calm and patient, showing she is still there.

grounding: A five-year-old insists on doing things alone, hides tears and avoids a hug, while her mother waits nearby until she accepts help.

passage: On sports day at the Shillong kindergarten, the other children ran to their parents after the sack race. Lalremsiami, five, walked to the water table alone and poured her own cup, spilling half. "I can do it," she told Mr Francis before he could help. Her mother hadn't been able to come. When she tripped on the way back, she jumped up fast, eyes wet, and wiped them hard. Mr Francis crouched and opened his arms. She shook her head and stepped away. "Okay," he said. "Want to hold the finish-line ribbon with me instead?" She nodded and took one end.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami pour at the water table?
qa.a: She poured her own cup of water, spilling half.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami be feeling when she wipes her eyes hard?
qa.a: She is likely hurt and disappointed, perhaps that her mother couldn't come, but she wants to hide it.

qa.q: What did Mr Francis offer after she refused the hug, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: He offered to let her hold the finish-line ribbon with him, which gave her closeness without the hug she didn't want.

qa.q: How might Mr Francis see Lalremsiami's "I can do it"?
qa.a: He may sense that her independence is also a shield, so he stays close in a way she can accept.

grounding: At a kindergarten sports day, a five-year-old insists on managing alone, hides tears and refuses a hug, and a teacher offers closeness another way.
